Rainfall is abundant, annually averaging 1,658 millimeters (65.3 in). It is especially common in the warmer months averaging 292 millimeters (11.5 in) in January and decreases in winter, averaging 32 millimeters (1.3 in).[[92]](#cite_note-INMETprecip-92) Neither São Paulo nor the nearby coast has ever been hit by a [tropical cyclone](/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone") and [tornadic](/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") activity is uncommon. During late winter, especially August, the city experiences the phenomenon known as *"veranico"* or *"verãozinho"* ("little summer"), which consists of hot and dry weather, sometimes reaching temperatures well above 28 °C (82 °F). On the other hand, relatively cool days during summer are fairly common when persistent winds blow from the ocean. On such occasions daily high temperatures may not surpass 20 °C (68 °F), accompanied by lows often below 15 °C (59 °F), however, spring and summer can be extremely hot when a heat wave hits the city followed by temperatures around 34 °C (93 °F), but in places with greater skyscraper density and less tree cover, the temperature can feel like 39 °C (102 °F), as on [Paulista Avenue](/wiki/Paulista_Avenue "Paulista Avenue") for example. In the summer of 2014, São Paulo was affected by a heat wave that lasted for almost 4 weeks with highs above 30 °C (86 °F), peaking on 36 °C (97 °F). Secondary to [deforestation](/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation"), [groundwater pollution](/wiki/Groundwater_pollution "Groundwater pollution"), and [climate change](/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), São Paulo is increasingly susceptible to [drought](/wiki/Drought "Drought") and [water shortages](/wiki/Water_shortage "Water shortage").[[93]](#cite_note-93)

The Inca estate of [Machu Picchu](/wiki/Machu_Picchu "Machu Picchu"), [Peru](/wiki/Peru "Peru"), is one of the [New Seven Wonders of the World](/wiki/New_Seven_Wonders_of_the_World#Winners "New Seven Wonders of the World").

The rise of plant growing and the subsequent appearance of permanent human settlements allowed for the multiple and overlapping beginnings of civilizations in South America.

One of the earliest known South American civilizations was [Caral–Supe](/wiki/Caral%E2%80%93Supe "Caral–Supe"), on the central Peruvian coast. Though a pre-ceramic culture, the monumental architecture of Caral–Supe created one of the first cities of the world, generally dated to around 3500 BC, at [Huaricanga](/wiki/Huaricanga "Huaricanga") in the [Fortaleza](/wiki/Fortaleza_River_(Peru) "Fortaleza River (Peru)") area, contemporaneous with the pyramids of [Ancient Egypt](/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt"), one of the [oldest-known civilizations](/wiki/Cradle_of_civilization "Cradle of civilization") in the Americas and one of the six sites where civilization separately originated in the ancient world.[[20]](#cite_note-AncientAndes-31) Caral–Supe governing class established a trade network and developed agriculture then followed by [Chavín](/wiki/Chav%C3%ADn "Chavín") by 900 BC, according to some estimates and archaeological finds. Artifacts were found at a site called [Chavín de Huantar](/wiki/Chav%C3%ADn_de_Huantar "Chavín de Huantar") in modern Peru at an elevation of 3,177 meters (10,423 ft). Singapore's main territory looks like a diamond-shaped island, although its territory includes surrounding smaller islands. The farthest outlying island is [Pedra Branca](/wiki/Pedra_Branca,_Singapore "Pedra Branca, Singapore"). Of Singapore's dozens of smaller islands, [Jurong Island](/wiki/Jurong_Island "Jurong Island"), [Pulau Tekong](/wiki/Pulau_Tekong "Pulau Tekong"), [Pulau Ubin](/wiki/Pulau_Ubin "Pulau Ubin") and [Sentosa](/wiki/Sentosa "Sentosa") are the larger ones. Most of Singapore is no more than 15 meters above sea level.

The highest point of Singapore is [Bukit Timah Hill](/wiki/Bukit_Timah_Hill "Bukit Timah Hill"), with a height from the ground of 164 m (538  ft) and made up of [igneous rock](/wiki/Igneous_rock "Igneous rock"), [granite](/wiki/Granite "Granite"). Hills and valleys of [sedimentary rock](/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") dominate the northwest, while the eastern region consists of [sandy](/wiki/Sand "Sand") and flatter land. Singapore has no natural lakes, but reservoirs and [water catchment areas](/wiki/Water_catchment_area "Water catchment area") have been constructed to store fresh water for [Singapore's water supply](/wiki/Water_resources_of_Singapore "Water resources of Singapore").
